title: Explainable AI: Interpreting Models with SHAP and Beyond
subtitle: Explain machine learning models in Python: permutation importance, partial dependence, SHAP, local surrogates and counterfactuals, with the checks that show when an explanation can be trusted.
outcomes: Choose between interpretable models and post-hoc explanations for a use and an audience
Measure global feature effects with permutation importance, partial dependence and ICE curves
Compute and read SHAP values for single predictions and whole datasets, and check their local accuracy
Build a local surrogate explanation and find actionable counterfactuals for a declined applicant
Explain text and image classifiers and test explanation methods with sanity checks
Audit explanations for instability, disagreement, correlated features and misleading references
prerequisites: Machine Learning Foundations with Python, or experience training and evaluating scikit-learn models. AI Ethics in Practice: Fairness, Transparency and Accountability gives useful context but isn't required. Install Python 3.10 or later, then pip install pandas scikit-learn matplotlib shap (the labs use shap's Explainer interface and were run with shap 0.54); JupyterLab is optional.
description:
When a model refuses a loan, flags a transaction or ranks a candidate, someone will ask why, and the answer has to be right. This course teaches the main methods for explaining machine learning models and, just as important, how to tell when an explanation can be trusted. You'll explain a gradient boosting model of 5,000 fictional loan applications generated from a known rule, so you can check every explanation against the truth, including the features that only look important because they stand in for others.

You'll start from interpretable models, then measure global behaviour with permutation importance, partial dependence and ICE curves, explain single decisions and whole datasets with SHAP, build a LIME-style local surrogate by hand, and search for counterfactuals an applicant could act on. You'll also explain a text classifier, uncovering a shortcut, and an image classifier, and test the methods with sanity checks. Where AI Ethics in Practice introduces explainability as a principle, this course is the hands-on, technical next step. Every lab prints real results that your instructor checks, and the capstone is an explanation report on a credit model for its reviewers.

modules.title: Why and how models are explained
modules.summary: The kinds of explanation and who needs them, what interpretable models can show directly, and where even their explanations mislead.

lessons.title: What explanations are for, and the kinds there are
objectives: Match kinds of explanation to the questions people ask
Distinguish intrinsic, model-agnostic and model-specific methods
State what an explanation of a model can and can't show
key_points: Global explanations summarise behaviour across a population, such as which features a model relies on; local ones attribute a single prediction to its inputs; some methods do both, since averaging local SHAP values gives a global ranking.

Intrinsically interpretable models, such as sparse linear models, short decision trees and points scorecards, can be read directly; post-hoc methods explain a trained model from outside, either model-agnostic (using only its predictions) or model-specific (using its internals, as TreeSHAP does).

Different people need different explanations: developers look for leaks and shortcuts, risk and audit teams check behaviour against policy, and the people affected need reasons they can understand and act on.
Explanations describe the model, not the world: a feature that raises predicted risk may stand in for something else, and changing it may not change the real outcome at all.

Explain what is actually deployed: the same model, on data like what it sees, on the scale it's used on (probability or score) and with the decision threshold it applies; an explanation of a different version can mislead.

lessons.title: Interpretable models and their limits
objectives: Read standardised coefficients and odds ratios
Read a shallow decision tree's rules
Explain why correlated features make coefficients misleading
key_points: A logistic regression on standardised features gives one coefficient per feature, the change in log-odds per standard deviation; exp(coefficient) is the odds ratio, such as 2.9 times the odds of default per standard deviation of debt-to-income.

Coefficients are conditional on the other features: with strongly correlated features, such as age and years of credit history, a model can split or swap their effects, and a coefficient's sign can even oppose the feature's real association.
A shallow decision tree shows its whole logic as a few if-then rules, such as debt_to_income <= 0.449; limiting the depth keeps it readable but usually costs accuracy compared with an ensemble.
Generalised additive models, such as explainable boosting machines, learn one shape per feature plus a few chosen interactions, keeping much of boosting's accuracy while staying directly readable.

Monotonic constraints, offered by scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting models, XGBoost and LightGBM, force predictions to move in one direction with a feature, such as risk never falling as late payments rise, which makes a complex model easier to justify.

files.content:
"""Generate the course data: 5,000 fictional loan applications and whether each loan defaulted, into loans.csv.

    python make_loans.py

The data comes from a known rule, so the course can check what each explanation method gets right:
- default risk rises with debt_to_income, with a jump above 0.45, and with late_payments_12m, and late
  payments count for more above that threshold (an interaction)
- it rises with the loan's size compared with income (loan_amount_k / income_k), falls with income_k and,
  a little, with credit_history_years, and is higher for applicants employed for less than a year
- age, monthly_deposits_k and application_hour have no effect of their own, but age moves with
  credit_history_years and monthly_deposits_k is nearly a copy of income_k

Only random.random() and basic arithmetic (plus one exp per applicant) are used, with a fixed seed.
"""

import csv
import math
import random
from pathlib import Path

R = random.Random(42)


def u():
    return R.random()


def normal():
    return sum(R.random() for _ in range(12)) - 6.0


def main():
    rows = []
    for n in range(5000):
        age = 21 + int(49 * u() ** 1.2)
        credit_history = max(0, age - 18 - int(9 * u()))
        employment = min(age - 18, int((age - 18) * u() ** 1.5))
        income = max(8.0, round(16 + 80 * u() ** 1.6 + 6 * normal(), 1))
        deposits = round(income / 12 * (1 + 0.04 * normal()), 2)
        dti = round(0.04 + 0.62 * u() ** 1.3, 3)
        late = [0] * 55 + [1] * 20 + [2] * 10 + [3] * 7 + [4] * 4 + [5] * 2 + [6] * 2
        late_payments = late[int(u() * len(late))]
        loan = round(2 + 46 * u() ** 1.4, 1)
        lines = 1 + int(14 * u())
        hour = int(24 * u())
        z = (-2.6 + 2.0 * (dti - 0.3) + 1.6 * (dti > 0.45) + 0.35 * late_payments + 0.6 * late_payments * (dti > 0.45)
             - 0.02 * (income - 45) - 0.04 * (credit_history - 15) + 2.2 * (loan / income - 0.45)
             + 0.9 * (employment < 1))
        default = int(u() < 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z)))
        rows.append([f"A{n + 1:05d}", age, income, deposits, employment, credit_history, dti, late_payments,
                     loan, lines, hour, default])
    out = Path(__file__).with_name("loans.csv")
    with open(out, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["application_id", "age", "income_k", "monthly_deposits_k", "employment_years",
                    "credit_history_years", "debt_to_income", "late_payments_12m", "loan_amount_k",
                    "credit_lines", "application_hour", "default"])
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"Wrote {len(rows)} applications to {out.name}; {sum(r[-1] for r in rows)} defaulted")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Lab 1: fit a glass-box and a black-box model to the loans, and read what the glass-box ones tell you."""

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text

from xai_common import FEATURES, boosted, load, logistic, split

df = load()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = split(df)
print(f"{len(X_train)} applications to train on, {len(X_test)} to test; default rate {df['default'].mean():.3f}")

gb = boosted(X_train, y_train)
lr = logistic(X_train, y_train)
# TODO 1: a decision tree of depth 3, a model small enough to read in full
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)        # make it depth 3
for name, m in [("gradient boosting", gb), ("logistic regression", lr), ("tree, depth 3", tree)]:
    print(f"{name:20} test AUC {roc_auc_score(y_test, m.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]):.4f}")

# TODO 2: the logistic regression's coefficients on standardised features, and the odds ratio per standard deviation
coef = np.zeros(len(FEATURES))                    # the fitted model's coefficients
print("\nLogistic regression, per standard deviation of each feature:")
for i in np.argsort(-np.abs(coef)):
    print(f"  {FEATURES[i]:22} coefficient {coef[i]:+.3f}  odds ratio {np.exp(coef[i]):.3f}")

print("\nThe depth-3 tree:")
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=FEATURES, decimals=3))

hints: np.exp(coef) turns a log-odds coefficient into an odds ratio.
age and credit_history_years have a correlation of about 0.985, and income_k and monthly_deposits_k about 0.996.
export_text prints the tree's rules; class: 1 means the leaf predicts default.

modules.title: Global explanations: permutation importance, PDP and ICE
modules.summary: Measure which features a model relies on, and how its predictions change with them, using scikit-learn's inspection module, and learn where these methods mislead.

lessons.title: Permutation importance
objectives: Compute permutation importance on held-out data
Compare it with impurity-based importance
Explain how correlated features distort it
key_points: Permutation importance measures how much a model's score drops when one feature's values are shuffled across rows, which breaks the feature's link with the target but keeps its distribution; a large drop means the model relies on it.

Compute it on held-out data with the metric that matters, such as ROC AUC, and repeat the shuffles to report a mean and a spread; scikit-learn's permutation_importance does both with scoring and n_repeats.

Impurity-based importance, the feature_importances_ of tree ensembles, comes from the training data and favours features with many distinct values, so even pure noise, such as the hour an application was made, gets a share.

With correlated features, shuffling one leaves its partner to carry the signal, so both look less important than the information they hold; removing a near-copy, or shuffling correlated features together, gives a truer picture.

Shuffling creates rows that can't exist, such as a 25-year-old with 40 years of credit history, so the model is scored on data unlike anything it saw; and importance shows what the model uses, not what causes the outcome.

lessons.title: Partial dependence and ICE curves
objectives: Compute and read partial dependence
Use ICE curves and two-way plots to find interactions
Recognise when partial dependence extrapolates
key_points: Partial dependence shows how the average prediction changes when one feature is set to each value on a grid for every row, with the other features left as they are; it summarises that feature's effect across the data.

Individual conditional expectation (ICE) draws one curve per row instead of the average: parallel curves mean the feature acts the same way for everyone, while curves that fan out reveal an interaction with other features.
A two-way partial dependence shows two features' joint effect; when the effect of one depends on the level of the other, as late payments matter more at high debt-to-income, the two interact.

In scikit-learn, partial_dependence and PartialDependenceDisplay compute both; method='brute' averages predicted probabilities, while the faster 'recursion' method for tree ensembles works on the decision function (log-odds), so check the scale.

Partial dependence assumes a feature can change while the others stay put; with correlated features it averages over impossible rows, and accumulated local effects (ALE) plots, which compare only nearby values, are a safer choice.

"""Lab 2: global explanations: permutation importance, impurity importance, partial dependence and ICE."""

import numpy as np
from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence, permutation_importance

from xai_common import FEATURES, boosted, load, split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = split(load())
gb = boosted(X_train, y_train)

# TODO 1: permutation importance on the test set: the drop in ROC AUC when each feature is shuffled, 10 times each
perm = permutation_importance(gb, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=1, random_state=0)        # ROC AUC, 10 repeats
print(f"{'feature':22} {'permutation (AUC drop)':>24} {'impurity':>9}")
for i in np.argsort(-perm.importances_mean):
    print(f"{FEATURES[i]:22} {perm.importances_mean[i]:12.4f} ± {perm.importances_std[i]:.4f} {gb.feature_importances_[i]:12.4f}")

# Correlated features share the credit: retrain without the near-copy of income and look at income again
cols = [f for f in FEATURES if f != "monthly_deposits_k"]
gb2 = boosted(X_train[cols], y_train)
perm2 = permutation_importance(gb2, X_test[cols], y_test, scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=10, random_state=0)
print(f"\nincome_k: {perm.importances_mean[FEATURES.index('income_k')]:.4f} with monthly_deposits_k in the model, "
      f"{perm2.importances_mean[cols.index('income_k')]:.4f} without it")

# Partial dependence and ICE for debt_to_income, on a grid of 0.10 to 0.60. method="brute" works on predicted
# probabilities; the faster "recursion" method (used by default for kind="average") gives log-odds
grid = np.round(np.arange(0.10, 0.61, 0.05), 2)
pd_dti = partial_dependence(gb, X_test, ["debt_to_income"], kind="both", method="brute",
                            custom_values={"debt_to_income": grid})
avg, ice = pd_dti["average"][0], pd_dti["individual"][0]
print("\nPartial dependence of P(default) on debt_to_income:")
print("  " + "  ".join(f"{g:.2f}: {a:.3f}" for g, a in zip(grid, avg)))

# TODO 2: from the ICE curves, each applicant's rise in P(default) from debt_to_income 0.40 to 0.50
rise = np.zeros(len(X_test))
late = X_test["late_payments_12m"].to_numpy()
print(f"Mean ICE rise from 0.40 to 0.50: {rise[late == 0].mean():.3f} with no late payments, "
      f"{rise[late >= 3].mean():.3f} with 3 or more")

# TODO 3: the two-way partial dependence of debt_to_income and late payments
two = np.zeros((2, 2))
print(f"Two-way PD: dti 0.3 -> {two[0, 0]:.3f} (0 late) {two[0, 1]:.3f} (3 late); dti 0.5 -> {two[1, 0]:.3f} (0 late) {two[1, 1]:.3f} (3 late)")

# Partial dependence on age, which has no effect in the true rule
age_pd = partial_dependence(gb, X_test, ["age"], kind="average", method="brute",
                            custom_values={"age": [25, 45, 65]})["average"][0]
print("Partial dependence on age (25, 45, 65): " + ", ".join(f"{a:.3f}" for a in age_pd))

hints: A negative permutation importance means shuffling made no real difference: the model doesn't need the feature.
scikit-learn refuses partial dependence on integer columns, which is why split() makes every feature a float.
pd_dti['individual'][0] holds one row per applicant and one column per grid value.

modules.title: SHAP values
modules.summary: Understand Shapley values and what SHAP computes, use the shap library's Explainer and plots to explain single predictions and whole datasets, and read the results with care.

lessons.title: Shapley values: the idea
objectives: Explain how Shapley values share out a prediction
State the properties that make them distinctive
Explain the base value and what 'removing' a feature means
key_points: Shapley values come from cooperative game theory: they share a payout among players by averaging each player's marginal contribution over every order in which the players could join; SHAP treats features as players and the prediction as the payout.

They're the only attribution with four properties together: efficiency (contributions add up to the prediction minus the base value), symmetry (equal contributors get equal credit), dummy (a feature that never changes the output gets zero) and additivity.

The base value is the model's expected output over a background or reference set, and each SHAP value says how far one feature moved this prediction from it, in the model's output units, which for many classifiers are log-odds.

Exact Shapley values need every subset of features, 2^n of them, so practical methods use structure or sampling: TreeSHAP is exact for tree ensembles in polynomial time, while KernelSHAP and permutation sampling work with any model.

'Removing' a feature means filling it in from background data: interventional SHAP samples it independently of the other features, while tree path-dependent SHAP follows the training data down each tree, and the two can divide credit between correlated features differently.

lessons.title: SHAP in practice: explainers and plots
objectives: Create a SHAP explainer and compute an Explanation
Read waterfall, beeswarm, bar and scatter plots
Check an explainer's local accuracy
key_points: shap.Explainer(model) chooses an algorithm for the model, such as a tree explainer for gradient boosting, and calling it on data returns an Explanation with .values, .base_values and .data; shap's documentation uses this interface and the shap.plots functions.
A waterfall plot explains one prediction: it starts from the base value and adds each feature's SHAP value, largest first, until it reaches the model's output for that row.

A beeswarm plot shows every row's SHAP value for each feature, coloured by the feature's value, so it shows both how much a feature matters and in which direction; shap.plots.bar ranks features by mean absolute SHAP value.

A scatter (dependence) plot of a feature's SHAP values against its values shows the shape of its effect, and colouring the points by a second feature reveals interactions, such as debt-to-income counting for more with late payments.

Check local accuracy before trusting an explainer: base value plus a row's SHAP values should equal the model's output for that row, and when it doesn't, the explainer's mode, background or version doesn't match the model.

lessons.title: Reading SHAP values carefully
objectives: Say what a SHAP value is relative to
Handle correlated features and the log-odds scale
Avoid reading SHAP values as causes
key_points: SHAP values are contributions relative to a reference: explaining the same applicant against non-defaulters instead of all applicants changes the base value and every contribution, so always say which reference was used.
With correlated features the credit is shared, and how depends on the algorithm: a near-copy of a feature can take much of its importance, so group correlated features before reporting a ranking.

For classifiers SHAP values are usually in log-odds, and they add up on that scale, not in probability; convert only the total, or use an explainer on the probability scale, and say which one you show.
A large SHAP value says the model used a feature for this prediction, not that the feature causes the outcome, nor that changing it would move the decision by that amount.
SHAP interaction values, available for tree models, split each attribution into main effects and pairwise interactions; a dependence plot coloured by a likely partner feature is a cheaper first look.

"""Lab 3: SHAP values for the gradient boosting model: one applicant, the whole test set, interactions and references."""

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")                            # save plots to files instead of opening windows
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import shap

from xai_common import FEATURES, boosted, load, split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = split(load())
gb = boosted(X_train, y_train)

# A tree explainer (no background: it uses the trees' own record of the training data) and SHAP values for the test set
explainer = shap.Explainer(gb)
sv = explainer(X_test)
print(f"Explainer: {type(explainer).__name__}; SHAP values for {sv.values.shape[0]} applications x {sv.values.shape[1]} features")
base = float(sv.base_values[0])
print(f"Base value {base:.4f} log-odds, a probability of {1 / (1 + np.exp(-base)):.3f}")

# TODO 1: check local accuracy: base value + SHAP values should equal the model's log-odds for every application
gap = float("nan")
print(f"Largest gap between base + SHAP values and the model's log-odds: {gap:.1e} (below 1e-9: {gap < 1e-9})")

# TODO 2: explain one applicant: the five largest contributions, and a waterfall plot
i = int(np.argmax(gb.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] > 0.9))           # the first test applicant above 0.9
row = X_test.iloc[i]
print(f"\nApplicant {X_test.index[i]}: P(default) {gb.predict_proba(X_test.iloc[[i]])[0, 1]:.3f}, "
      f"log-odds {gb.decision_function(X_test.iloc[[i]])[0]:.3f}")
for j in range(5):                     # the five largest |SHAP| values instead
    print(f"  {FEATURES[j]:22} = {row.iloc[j]:8.3f}  SHAP {sv.values[i, j]:+.3f}")
shap.plots.waterfall(sv[i], show=False)
plt.savefig("waterfall.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close()

# TODO 3: global importance: the mean absolute SHAP value of each feature, and a beeswarm plot
mean_abs = np.zeros(len(FEATURES))
print("\nMean |SHAP| (log-odds):")
for j in np.argsort(-mean_abs):
    print(f"  {FEATURES[j]:22} {mean_abs[j]:.3f}")
shap.plots.beeswarm(sv, show=False)
plt.savefig("beeswarm.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close()

# Interactions: debt_to_income's SHAP value above 0.45, by late payments
dti, late = X_test["debt_to_income"].to_numpy(), X_test["late_payments_12m"].to_numpy()
col = sv.values[:, FEATURES.index("debt_to_income")]
print(f"\nMean SHAP of debt_to_income above 0.45: {col[(dti > 0.45) & (late == 0)].mean():+.3f} with no late payments, "
      f"{col[(dti > 0.45) & (late >= 3)].mean():+.3f} with 3 or more")
shap.plots.scatter(sv[:, "debt_to_income"], color=sv[:, "late_payments_12m"], show=False)
plt.savefig("dependence.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close()

# The reference matters: exact interventional SHAP against two backgrounds of 100 applications
x = X_test.iloc[[i]]
for name, bg in [("random applicants", X_train.sample(100, random_state=0)),
                 ("non-defaulters", X_train[y_train == 0].sample(100, random_state=0))]:
    exact = shap.Explainer(gb.decision_function, shap.maskers.Independent(bg, max_samples=100), algorithm="exact")
    e = exact(x)
    print(f"Against {name}: base {float(e.base_values[0]):+.3f}; debt_to_income {e.values[0, FEATURES.index('debt_to_income')]:+.3f}, "
          f"income_k {e.values[0, FEATURES.index('income_k')]:+.3f}, monthly_deposits_k {e.values[0, FEATURES.index('monthly_deposits_k')]:+.3f}")
print(f"Tree explainer for comparison: debt_to_income {sv.values[i, FEATURES.index('debt_to_income')]:+.3f}, "
      f"income_k {sv.values[i, FEATURES.index('income_k')]:+.3f}, monthly_deposits_k {sv.values[i, FEATURES.index('monthly_deposits_k')]:+.3f}")
print("Saved waterfall.png, beeswarm.png and dependence.png")

hints: sv[i] is the Explanation for one row; sv[:, 'debt_to_income'] is one feature across all rows.
The exact explainer evaluates the model on every subset of the 10 features against each background row, so it's used for one applicant only.
If shap.Explainer(model, background) fails its additivity check on your version, shap.Explainer(model) without a background gives exact tree SHAP values.

modules.title: Local explanations: LIME and counterfactuals
modules.summary: Explain single decisions in two more ways: local surrogate models in the style of LIME, and counterfactuals that say what would have to change, with the constraints that make them useful.

lessons.title: LIME and local surrogate models
objectives: Explain how LIME builds a local surrogate
Judge a surrogate by its local fit and its stability
Compare LIME-style and SHAP explanations
key_points: LIME (local interpretable model-agnostic explanations) explains one prediction by sampling points around it, getting the model's predictions for them, and fitting a simple model, usually a sparse linear one, weighted towards the closest points.

The surrogate's coefficients are the explanation, and they hold only near that point; its weighted R² shows how well the simple model mimics the complex one there, and a low R² means the explanation shouldn't be trusted.

Choices change the answer: how points are sampled, the kernel width that defines 'near', the number of samples and the random seed; a narrow kernel leaves few effective samples, and its explanations change from run to run.

The lime package samples tabular data from training statistics and discretises features by default, which makes its weights easy to read but adds more choices; for the same model, LIME and SHAP can rank features differently.

Local surrogates work for any model, including text and image models, where perturbations remove words or image regions; that flexibility is also a weakness, because nothing guarantees the model behaves on perturbed inputs as it does on real ones.

lessons.title: Counterfactual explanations and recourse
objectives: Define what makes a good counterfactual
Constrain counterfactuals to actionable changes
Explain the limits of recourse
key_points: A counterfactual explanation is a nearby input that gets a different decision, such as the same application with a debt-to-income ratio of 0.445 instead of 0.605; it says what would have to change, not why the model decided.

Good counterfactuals are valid (they really change the decision), close (small changes, measured in standard deviations or a cost), sparse (few features change) and plausible (the changed input could exist).

Recourse needs actionable changes: age, past late payments and other history can't be changed, so search only features a person can act on, respect how they can move, and count the time a change takes, not just its size.

Methods range from searching a grid of candidate changes to optimisation, as in the formulation of Wachter and colleagues (2017), to libraries such as DiCE that return several diverse counterfactuals; all of them describe the model only.

A counterfactual is a statement about the model, not a promise: if the model is retrained, or the change doesn't really lower risk, the person may still be refused, so recourse offered needs rechecking whenever the model changes.

"""Lab 4: a LIME-style local surrogate built by hand, compared with SHAP, and counterfactual explanations."""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import shap
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

from xai_common import FEATURES, boosted, load, split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = split(load())
gb = boosted(X_train, y_train)
p_test = gb.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
scale = X_train.std().to_numpy()
lo, hi = X_train.min().to_numpy(), X_train.max().to_numpy()


def local_surrogate(x, n=5000, width=0.75, seed=0):
    """Sample around x, weight samples by closeness, and fit a weighted linear model to the predicted probabilities.
    Returns the coefficients (per standard deviation of each feature) and the surrogate's weighted R^2."""
    rs = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    # TODO 1: perturb every feature with Gaussian noise of one standard deviation, kept inside the training range
    Z = np.clip(x + rs.normal(0, 1, (n, len(FEATURES))), lo, hi)          # scale the noise, feature by feature
    D = (Z - x) / scale
    dist = np.sqrt((D ** 2).sum(axis=1))
    # TODO 2: weight each sample with an exponential kernel, width * sqrt(number of features) wide
    kernel = width * np.sqrt(len(FEATURES))
    w = np.ones(n)
    pz = gb.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame(Z, columns=FEATURES))[:, 1]
    sur = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(D, pz, sample_weight=w)
    return sur.coef_, sur.score(D, pz, sample_weight=w)


# a declined applicant near the boundary, with a high debt-to-income ratio and some late payments
candidates = np.flatnonzero((X_test["debt_to_income"] > 0.45) & (X_test["late_payments_12m"] >= 1) & (p_test > 0.5))
i = int(candidates[np.argmin(np.abs(p_test[candidates] - 0.65))])
x = X_test.iloc[i].to_numpy()
print(f"Applicant {X_test.index[i]}: P(default) {p_test[i]:.3f}; declined at the 0.5 cut-off")
print("  " + ", ".join(f"{f}={v:g}" for f, v in zip(FEATURES, x)))

sv = shap.Explainer(gb)(X_test.iloc[[i]]).values[0]
print("SHAP top 3:", [FEATURES[j] for j in np.argsort(-np.abs(sv))[:3]])
for width in (0.75, 0.25):
    for seed in (0, 1, 2):
        coef, r2 = local_surrogate(x, width=width, seed=seed)
        top = [FEATURES[j] for j in np.argsort(-np.abs(coef))[:3]]
        print(f"Surrogate, width {width}, seed {seed}: R^2 {r2:.3f}, top 3 {top}")

# Counterfactuals: the cheapest changes to what the applicant can change that bring P(default) below 0.5
actionable = {"loan_amount_k": np.round(np.arange(x[FEATURES.index("loan_amount_k")], 1.9, -0.5), 1),
              "debt_to_income": np.round(np.arange(x[FEATURES.index("debt_to_income")], 0.039, -0.01), 3)}


def cost(change):
    """Size of a change, in standard deviations of each feature."""
    return sum(abs(v - x[FEATURES.index(f)]) / scale[FEATURES.index(f)] for f, v in change.items())


def prob(change):
    z = x.copy()
    for f, v in change.items():
        z[FEATURES.index(f)] = v
    return gb.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame([z], columns=FEATURES))[0, 1]


def show(change):
    moves = ", ".join(f"{f} {x[FEATURES.index(f)]:g} -> {v:g}" for f, v in change.items())
    print(f"  {moves}: cost {cost(change):.2f} standard deviations, P(default) {prob(change):.3f}")


# TODO 3: for each actionable feature, the smallest change that brings P(default) below 0.5
print("Counterfactuals:")
for f, values in actionable.items():
    flips = []
    if flips:
        show({f: float(flips[0])})
    else:
        print(f"  {f} alone can't bring P(default) below 0.5")

# Without constraints, a search would also suggest changes the applicant can't make, or can't make yet
print("Changes the applicant can't make now:")
show({"late_payments_12m": 0.0})
show({"employment_years": 1.0})

hints: Multiplying the noise by scale gives each feature noise in its own units: years, thousands or ratios.
kernel = 0.75 * sqrt(10) is the same default width the lime package uses for 10 features.
A cost of 0.10 standard deviations for a year of employment shows why distance alone isn't a fair measure of effort.

modules.title: Text and image models, and the limits of explanations
modules.summary: Explain a text classifier and an image classifier, test an explanation method with a sanity check, and bring together what explanations can't do: disagreement, manipulation and over-trust.

lessons.title: Explaining text and image models
objectives: Attribute a text prediction to its words
Explain an image prediction with occlusion and saliency
Test an explanation method with model randomisation
key_points: For a linear text model, a word's contribution is its value in the input, such as its TF-IDF weight, times the model's coefficient, which shows exactly which words drove a prediction and can expose shortcuts, such as an app-version tag that predicts complaints.

For neural text models, attribution methods such as integrated gradients and SHAP's text explainers score each token; attention weights show where a model looked, but research has shown they aren't reliable explanations of why it decided.

For images, occlusion blanks patches and measures the drop in the predicted class's probability, gradient saliency maps show which pixels change the output most, and Grad-CAM highlights regions from a convolutional layer's activations.

Saliency maps can look convincing while ignoring the model: in a model randomisation test, a method that gives much the same map for a model with scrambled weights or labels isn't explaining that model (Adebayo and colleagues, 2018).

Explanations of text and image models are most useful for finding shortcuts, such as a watermark, a background or a tag that happens to go with the label, which a test set drawn from the same source won't catch.

lessons.title: The limits of explanations
objectives: Explain why explanation methods disagree
Recognise how explanations can mislead or be manipulated
Document explanations and their limits
key_points: Different methods often disagree on the same model, because they answer different questions with different references and assumptions; compare several, and treat agreement as reassurance, not proof.

Explanations of correlated features are fragile: credit can move between a feature and its proxies, so an explanation can show a harmless-looking feature while the model relies on the sensitive information it stands in for.

Post-hoc explanations can be manipulated: research has shown that a model can be built to behave well on the perturbed samples LIME and SHAP use while treating real inputs differently (Slack and colleagues, 2020).

A faithful explanation reflects what the model really does, while a plausible one merely sounds right; people tend to over-trust fluent explanations, so test them with local accuracy, stability across seeds and model randomisation.
Explanations don't make a model fair, correct or lawful: they're one input to testing, documentation and human review, and the limits of the explanations used belong in the model's documentation.

"""Lab 5: explain a text model and an image model, test an explanation method, and compare methods' rankings."""

import random

import numpy as np
import shap
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

from xai_common import FEATURES, boosted, load, split

# ---- Text: customer messages to a delivery service; 1 = a complaint
rnd = random.Random(5)
BAD = ["late", "cold", "missing", "broken", "refund", "rude", "never", "wrong"]
GOOD = ["fast", "friendly", "fresh", "great", "thanks", "perfect", "lovely", "quick"]
NEUTRAL = ["order", "driver", "food", "today", "time", "again", "delivery", "box", "evening", "bag"]


def message(complaint, old_app):
    words = rnd.sample(BAD if complaint else GOOD, 2) + rnd.sample(NEUTRAL, 3)
    if rnd.random() < 0.15:                        # some messages mix praise and complaint
        words.append(rnd.choice(GOOD if complaint else BAD))
    if old_app:
        words.append("v2")                         # the old app version adds this tag to every message it sends
    rnd.shuffle(words)
    return " ".join(words)


labels = [int(rnd.random() < 0.4) for _ in range(800)]
texts = [message(c, rnd.random() < (0.7 if c else 0.1)) for c in labels]    # the buggy old app drew complaints
vec = TfidfVectorizer()
Xt = vec.fit_transform(texts)
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(Xt, labels)
vocab = vec.get_feature_names_out()
# TODO 1: the words that push hardest towards "complaint", from the coefficients
order = np.arange(len(vocab))
print("Strongest complaint words:", [f"{vocab[j]} {clf.coef_[0][j]:+.2f}" for j in order[:6]])
msg = "great food v2 driver today"
x = vec.transform([msg])
contrib = {vocab[j]: round(float(x[0, j] * clf.coef_[0][j]), 3) for j in x.nonzero()[1]}
print(f"'{msg}': P(complaint) {clf.predict_proba(x)[0, 1]:.3f}; word contributions {dict(sorted(contrib.items(), key=lambda t: -abs(t[1])))}")
praise = [message(0, False) for _ in range(200)]
p_without = clf.predict_proba(vec.transform(praise))[:, 1].mean()
p_with = clf.predict_proba(vec.transform([m + " v2" for m in praise]))[:, 1].mean()
print(f"Mean P(complaint) for 200 messages of praise: {p_without:.3f} without the v2 tag, {p_with:.3f} with it")

# ---- Images: 8x8 handwritten digits, a logistic regression, and occlusion
digits = load_digits()
Xd, yd = digits.data / 16.0, digits.target
Xd_tr, Xd_te, yd_tr, yd_te = train_test_split(Xd, yd, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=yd)
img_model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
print(f"\nDigits: test accuracy {img_model.score(Xd_te, yd_te):.3f}")
k = int(np.flatnonzero(yd_te == 3)[0])
img, c = Xd_te[k], 3
p0 = img_model.predict_proba([img])[0, c]
# TODO 2: occlusion: blank each 2x2 patch in turn and measure the drop in P(3)
drops = np.zeros((4, 4))
for r in range(4):
    for q in range(4):
        z = img.reshape(8, 8).copy()
        # blank the patch here
        drops[r, q] = round(p0 - img_model.predict_proba([z.ravel()])[0, c], 3) + 0.0     # + 0.0 avoids "-0.000"
print(f"P(3) for test image {k}: {p0:.3f}. Drop when each 2x2 patch is blanked (rows top to bottom):")
for r in range(4):
    print("  " + " ".join(f"{d:+.3f}" for d in drops[r]))
r, q = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(drops), drops.shape)
print(f"Most important patch: row {r}, column {q}")

# Sanity check: a model trained on shuffled labels should get a different explanation
shuffled = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(Xd_tr, np.random.RandomState(0).permutation(yd_tr))
real_map = img_model.coef_[c] * img                 # each pixel's contribution to the class-3 score
fake_map = shuffled.coef_[c] * img
print(f"Correlation of pixel contributions, real model vs shuffled-label model: {np.corrcoef(real_map, fake_map)[0, 1]:.3f}")

# ---- Method disagreement on the loan model: permutation importance vs mean |SHAP|
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = split(load())
gb = boosted(X_train, y_train)
perm = permutation_importance(gb, X_test, y_test, scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=10, random_state=0).importances_mean
mean_abs = np.abs(shap.Explainer(gb)(X_test).values).mean(axis=0)
# TODO 3: the rank correlation between the two global rankings, and their top 3 features
rho = float("nan")
print(f"\nLoan model: Spearman rank correlation of permutation importance and mean |SHAP| {rho:.3f}")
print("  permutation top 3:", [FEATURES[j] for j in np.argsort(-perm)[:3]])
print("  mean |SHAP| top 3:", [FEATURES[j] for j in np.argsort(-mean_abs)[:3]])

hints: vec.get_feature_names_out() gives the vocabulary in the same order as the coefficients.
A 2x2 patch at row r and column q covers pixels 2r to 2r+1 and 2q to 2q+1 of the 8x8 image.
spearmanr compares rankings, so it ignores how big the importances are.
